questions.prompt: After `int fd[2]; pipe(fd);`, which descriptor do you READ from?
options: fd[0]
fd[1]
Either
Neither: pipes use stdin
questions.explain: `fd[0]` is the read end and `fd[1]` the write end.

questions.prompt: `fd[{{0}}]` is the read end of a pipe and `fd[{{1}}]` the write end.
What does `read` return when the pipe is empty and every write end has been closed?
options: The size of the buffer
It blocks forever
questions.explain: 0 means end of file. If a write end is still open somewhere, `read` blocks instead.

questions.prompt: A child loops on `read` from a pipe and never sees the end of the data, even though the parent has finished writing. Most likely cause?
options: The pipe is too small
Some process still has the write end open (for instance the parent, or the child itself)
The child must call `exec`
`read` cannot return 0 on a pipe
questions.explain: End of file arrives only when ALL copies of the write end are closed, in every process. Close the ends you do not use right after the fork.

questions.prompt: Which statements about pipes are true?
options: Data goes one way only
`read` blocks while the pipe is empty and writers exist
After a `fork` both processes have both ends open
One pipe is enough for a two-way conversation
questions.explain: A pipe is one-way: for a conversation make two. After `fork` each process should close the end it does not use.
option_notes: False: use two pipes, one for each direction.

questions.prompt: How many pipes do two processes need to talk in both directions?
options: It depends on the message size

questions.explain: The child writes three bytes (`h`, `i`, newline) into the pipe; the parent reads them, ends the string and prints it.

questions.prompt: Put the steps to run `ls | wc` without a shell in order.
items: `fork` the first child: `dup2(p[1], 1)`, close both ends, `exec ls`
`fork` the second child: `dup2(p[0], 0)`, close both ends, `exec wc`
The parent closes both ends of the pipe
The parent waits for both children
questions.explain: The pipe must exist before the forks so both children inherit it. The parent closes its own copies so that `wc` can see the end of its input.

options: Closes standard output
Makes descriptor 1 refer to the write end of the pipe
Creates a second pipe
Copies the contents of the pipe to the screen
questions.explain: After it, anything the process writes to its standard output (including after an `exec`) goes into the pipe.

questions.prompt: After `dup2(p[1], 1)` in a child, why do you also `close(p[1])`?
options: `dup2` needs it
Otherwise there is an extra, useless write end open and the reader may never get end of file
To free the memory of the pipe
It is only a good habit with no effect
questions.explain: Every open copy of the write end delays the end of file for the reader.

questions.prompt: Match each function with what it is used for in pipe programs.
pairs: creates the two ends of a pipe
makes one descriptor a copy of another
wraps a descriptor in a FILE *
takes bytes out of a pipe, blocking if empty
questions.explain: `fdopen` lets you use `fgets` and `fprintf` on a pipe end.

questions.prompt: Which situations can make a process that reads a pipe hang forever?
options: The writer never closes its end
The reader itself still holds the write end open
The writer closed its end after sending everything
A third process holds a copy of the write end
questions.explain: As long as ANY write end is open, `read` waits for more data.
option_notes: True: close the unused end in the reader.
False: that is the correct way to finish.

questions.prompt: Why must the pipe be created BEFORE the `fork`?
options: `fork` closes pipes made later
Each process would otherwise get its own, unrelated pipe
Pipes cannot be created in a child
There is no reason
questions.explain: The child inherits the descriptors that exist at the moment of the fork. A pipe made afterwards would be private to one of them.
